newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan shippers say politics won't sink China plan.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan shippers say politics won't sink China plan.

text.p: Taiwan shippers said on Tuesday they expected direct Taiwan-China shipping links to materialise in April, despite media reports saying rival Beijing's political concerns could delay progress.
"Hopes for direct shipping links with China have not changed and this is still expected to start in April," said an executive at Yangming Marine Transport Corp.

Taiwan media said China might delay the unveiling of a list of shippers approved for the first crossings of the Taiwan strait since 1949 to protest Taiwan's hosting of a controversial visit by Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama.
Taiwan's Commercial Daily on Tuesday quoted Li Xin, deputy Taiwan affairs chief in China's communications ministry, as saying Beijing would postpone the announcement but did not say for how long.
Taipei shippers said Beijing was still processing a batch of applications by Taiwan and mainland shippers eager to make direct crossings, but agreed that politics could intervene.
China would not make an announcement during the Dalai Lama's March 22-27 visit but could do so after the visit, they said.
Taiwan shippers' applications were sent to Beijing in early March for a review expected to take 45 days. Results should be known in April, shippers said.
Taiwan's Republic of China government, exiled from the mainland after losing a civil war in 1949, has banned direct shipping and other direct links since.

Anticipating a breakthrough, Taiwan shippers have scrambled to prepare ships for the short 300 km (180 mile) voyage between the ports tipped to pioneer the service -- Kaohsiung in southern Taiwan and Xiamen in southeastern Fujian province.

Despite the long-time prohibition on official contacts, indirect trade and Taiwan investment in the mainland have flourished since a political thaw began in the late 1980s -- prompting calls to ease the shipping ban.
Indirect transshipping across the Taiwan strait has soared in recent years, with Hong Kong cashing in as a middleman. Experts say direct shipments would be 40 percent cheaper.
